metaDesc: A budget day trip to Chachoengsao (Paet Riu) from Bangkok by train for just a few baht. Visit Luang Pho Sothon, walk the 100-year-old Ban Mai Market, eat khao pak mo noodles, plus a real budget breakdown and a follow-along schedule.

h1:
Chachoengsao on a Budget
Train, Temples & Old Markets
intro: Chachoengsao (locally called Paet Riu) is one of the best-value day trips near Bangkok, because you can take the train straight into the town centre. A third-class train ticket costs just a few baht, and you don't need your own car. This trip takes you to pay respects to Luang Pho Sothon, walk the 100-year-old Ban Mai Market, eat khao pak mo noodles by the Bang Pakong River, then visit the Ganesha shrine at Wat Saman. We've laid it out as a block-day plan with a real budget breakdown so you can see exactly what a full day here costs.

blocks.html: If you want a trip near Bangkok that won't drain your wallet, Paet Riu genuinely delivers. The best part is you don't need a car: just take the Eastern Line train from Hua Lamphong straight to Chachoengsao station. The fare is cheaper than a single cup of coffee, and the main sights — temples and markets — are an easy songthaew or motorbike-taxi ride apart within town. Both temples are free to enter, market food starts at well under 50 THB, and you can do the whole trip for a couple hundred baht per person.

blocks.text: Why Paet Riu is such great value on a budget

blocks.html: Three things make this trip genuinely cheap. First, it's only just over 60 km from Bangkok — about an hour and a half by train. Second, the railway station is right in the town centre, so a ride to Wat Sothon costs only a few baht. And third, the main attractions are temples and markets that are free to enter, so you're only paying for food and local transport — no pricey admission tickets like a theme park or museum.

items: Cheap to get there — a third-class train from Hua Lamphong/Lat Krabang to Chachoengsao costs around 10–15 THB, far less than a van or driving yourself.
Free temples — Wat Sothon and Wat Saman Rattanaram don't charge admission; you only pay for flowers and incense if you choose to make an offering.
Cheap market food — Ban Mai is a 100-year-old market where food starts at well under 50 THB, with khao pak mo noodles from 40 THB a plate.
No overnight needed — you can do it as a single day trip and skip accommodation entirely; if you'd rather take it slow, save some budget for one night.

blocks.text: How to get to Paet Riu by train

blocks.html: The Eastern Line runs from Bangkok station (Hua Lamphong) through Makkasan and Lat Krabang to Chachoengsao Junction, with several trains a day — ordinary, rapid, and express services. The third-class commuter trains have the cheapest fares and suit a budget trip best. If you live on the east side of Bangkok, boarding at Lat Krabang is closer and saves time.

items: Where to board — Bangkok station (Hua Lamphong) for commuter trains, or board at Lat Krabang if you're on the east side, which is closer.
How long it takes — Hua Lamphong to Chachoengsao is about 1.5 hours; Lat Krabang to Chachoengsao is about 40–50 min.
Ticket price — third class runs about 10–15 THB per trip; buy your ticket at the station counter, no advance booking needed.
Check the timetable first — schedules can change, so check the latest at the State Railway site (railway.co.th) or snap a photo of the station timetable so you don't miss your train back.

blocks.title: Plan your return train carefully
blocks.html: Evening trains back to Bangkok are limited. Before you leave Chachoengsao station in the morning, take a photo of the return timetable so you can pace your day and don't risk missing the last train home.

blocks.text: Getting around town on the cheap

blocks.html: Once you arrive at Chachoengsao station, the sights are in different corners of town. The cheapest way around is the yellow songthaews that run fixed routes for just a few baht. Wat Saman is a bit outside town, so if you're in a group it's better value to charter a songthaew or split a motorbike taxi than to call a Grab.

items: Station to Wat Sothon — a yellow songthaew costs about 8–10 THB and takes roughly 10 min.
Wat Sothon to Ban Mai Market — a short hop by songthaew or motorbike taxi for a few tens of baht.

Getting to Wat Saman Rattanaram — it's about 20–30 min outside town; if you're in a group, chartering a songthaew and splitting the cost is good value, or skip it for next time if you're on a tight budget.

blocks.text: A budget plan you can actually follow

blocks.html: We've laid out two options to suit your time and budget. The first is a single-day trip, out in the morning and back in the evening, with maximum savings. The second adds one overnight stay for anyone who wants to take it slow and catch the morning market the next day. One key point: Ban Mai Market only opens on weekends and public holidays, so if you want the full market experience, you'll need to go on a day off.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Morning out, evening back — maximum savings

items.activity: Board the train at Hua Lamphong or Lat Krabang
items.note: Buy a third-class ticket at the counter for a few baht, and snap a photo of the return timetable right away.

items.activity: Arrive at Chachoengsao station, take a songthaew to Wat Sothon
items.note: A yellow songthaew costs 8–10 THB. Wat Sothon is open roughly 07:00–16:30; mornings are still quiet.

items.activity: Pay respects to Luang Pho Sothon, photograph the marble ordination hall
items.note: No entry fee. Offering stalls ring the temple; flowers and incense sets cost just a few tens of baht.

items.activity: Take a ride to the 100-year-old Ban Mai Market
items.note: The market opens Sat–Sun and holidays, roughly 08:30–17:00, busiest 10:00–14:00.

items.activity: Eat a late-morning bowl of khao pak mo noodles, graze on riverside snacks
items.note: Famous market stalls serve khao pak mo from 40 THB a plate, sets around 70 THB. Walk and sample charcoal-oven sweets, kuychai dumplings, and sip old-style coffee by the Bang Pakong River.

items.activity: Choose: visit the Ganesha shrine at Wat Saman, or keep walking the market
items.note: In a group, chartering a songthaew to Wat Saman and splitting the cost is good value. The temple is open roughly 08:00–17:00, free entry. If you're keeping the budget tight, just keep exploring the market and head back.
Leave time for the ride back into town, and don't forget the return train time you photographed in the morning.

items.activity: Board the train back to Bangkok
items.note: You'll be home by evening, with no accommodation cost. The total per person stays in the low hundreds of baht.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Option: stay one night, take it slow

items.activity: Wake early and walk the in-town morning market for breakfast
items.note: If you stayed overnight in the town centre, there are morning markets and rice-soup shops for a cheap breakfast.

items.activity: Visit the Ganesha shrine at Wat Saman Rattanaram, unhurried
items.note: If you skipped it yesterday, go today to see the giant pink reclining Ganesha and walk around the base to pay respects to the various Ganesha poses.

items.activity: Relax at a Bang Pakong riverside cafe
items.note: This stretch has several cafes with river views; drinks run around 100 THB. A nice rest before heading home.

items.activity: Buy souvenirs and head back to the station
items.note: In mango season (Mar–May) you can take home nam dok mai mangoes, or pick up moon cakes and mu yo (Vietnamese sausage) as gifts.

items.activity: Board the train back to Bangkok
items.note: Check your return train ahead of time. Even with one overnight, the total stays manageable if you pick budget accommodation in town.

blocks.text: The real budget: what a full day actually costs

blocks.html: Here's an estimated per-person budget for a one-day return trip. These are rough figures and may shift depending on how much you eat and how many people split the rides, but the overall picture is clear: a full day in Paet Riu can genuinely be done for a couple hundred baht per person.

items: Round-trip train — about 20–30 THB (third class, 10–15 THB each way).
Songthaew/motorbike taxi in town — about 40–80 THB, depending on how many stops and whether you charter.
Food for the day — about 120–200 THB (khao pak mo noodles, sweets, coffee, market snacks).
Flowers and incense — about 30–60 THB, as you wish.
Approximate total per person — about 250–400 THB for a day trip with no overnight stay.

blocks.title: How to push the budget even lower
blocks.html: If you're in a group, chartering a songthaew and splitting it beats calling rides one by one, and eating at market stalls instead of air-conditioned sit-down places saves more. As for offerings, a small set is plenty — you don't need the big one to earn the same merit.

blocks.text: Cheap eats to try at Ban Mai Market

blocks.html: The heart of this budget trip is Ban Mai Market, a 100-year-old wooden market on the Bang Pakong River. Food here is friendly on the wallet, starting at well under 50 THB, and you can graze your way through savoury and sweet Thai-Chinese dishes. These are the eats people come here specifically for.

items.name: Khao pak mo (steamed rice noodles)
items.blurb: Paet Riu's signature dish — thin wrappers with a generous filling. Famous market stalls offer several fillings; from 40 THB a plate, or a set around 70 THB with several pieces and broth.

items.name: Kuychai & charcoal-oven sweets
items.blurb: Fragrant Thai sweets baked in a charcoal oven, plus thin-skinned kuychai dumplings packed with filling. A few baht apiece, perfect for grazing as you walk.

items.name: Old-style riverside coffee
items.blurb: A long-running coffee shop in the market, brewed the old-fashioned way. Sip it while watching the Bang Pakong River for a few tens of baht a glass.

blocks.text: Tips to get the most for your money

items: Go on a Saturday or Sunday, because Ban Mai Market only opens on weekends. On a weekday you'll only get the temples and miss the food highlights.
Reach Wat Sothon before 10am to avoid the crowds and harsh sun, and get nicer photos of the ordination hall.
Mango season runs roughly March–May, when Paet Riu is known for its nam dok mai mangoes — great to take home as gifts at orchard prices.
Bring water and a hat or umbrella, since the temple and market walks involve a fair bit of sun, and wear comfortable walking shoes.
If you have budget to spare and want to keep going, there are cheap hotels in town for one night, so you can take the next morning slow.

faq.q: How much is a train ticket to Chachoengsao?
faq.a: A third-class Eastern Line train from Hua Lamphong or Lat Krabang to Chachoengsao station costs around 10–15 THB per trip. Buy it at the station counter with no advance booking needed. The journey takes about 1.5 hours from Hua Lamphong, or 40–50 min from Lat Krabang.

faq.q: How much does a budget day in Chachoengsao cost?
faq.a: A day trip with no overnight stay runs about 250–400 THB per person, covering the round-trip train, songthaews in town, food for the day, and flowers and incense. Both temples are free to enter and market food starts at well under 50 THB, so it's easy to keep the budget down.

faq.q: Can I visit Paet Riu without a car?
faq.a: Easily. This trip is designed around taking the train into the town centre, then using yellow songthaews or motorbike taxis to get around. Wat Sothon and Ban Mai Market are close to town, while Wat Saman is a bit outside — if you're in a group, chartering a songthaew and splitting the cost is better value.

faq.q: When is Ban Mai Market open, and is the food cheap?
faq.a: Ban Mai Market only opens on weekends and public holidays, roughly 08:30–17:00, busiest 10:00–14:00. The food is friendly on the wallet: khao pak mo noodles from 40 THB a plate, sweets and old-style coffee for a few tens of baht — ideal for a budget trip.

faq.q: Should I go on a weekday or a weekend?
faq.a: A Saturday or Sunday is recommended, because Ban Mai Market only opens on weekends. On a weekday you'll only get the temples and miss the food highlights. If you want to avoid temple crowds, reach Wat Sothon before 10am.
